questions.enonce_markdown:
Briefly define the following;

(i) Joint demand.

(ii) Competitive demand.

(iii) Joint supply.

(iv) Competitive supply.

2+2+2+2=(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** These terms describe how the demand for, or the supply of, one good is linked to another good.

**(i) Joint demand (2 marks).** The **demand for two or more goods that are used together**, so that they are demanded at the same time. They are **complements**: a rise in the demand for one raises the demand for the other. Example: cars and petrol, or bread and butter.

**(ii) Competitive demand (2 marks).** The **demand for goods that are substitutes**, that is, goods that can be used in place of each other to satisfy the same want. A rise in the price of one makes consumers buy more of the other. Example: tea and coffee, or rice and bread.

**(iii) Joint supply (2 marks).** The situation where **the production of one good automatically produces another good** (a by-product), so that the two are supplied together. Example: beef and hides, or cotton lint and cotton seed. A rise in the supply of one raises the supply of the other.

**(iv) Competitive supply (2 marks).** The situation where **the same resources can be used to produce either of two goods**, so the goods compete for those resources. More of one good can be produced only by producing less of the other. Example: a farmer who can use the same land to grow maize or cassava.

questions.enonce_markdown:
State and explain Four (04) factors influencing the elasticity of demand for a commodity.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Price elasticity of demand measures how much the quantity demanded of a good changes when its price changes. Demand is **elastic** when the quantity demanded changes by a bigger proportion than the price, and **inelastic** when it changes by a smaller proportion. The main factors are the following.

1. **Availability and closeness of substitutes.** If there are many close substitutes (for example, one brand of soap for another), a rise in the price makes consumers switch, so demand is elastic. If there are no substitutes (for example, salt), demand is inelastic.

2. **Nature of the good: necessity or luxury.** Demand for necessities such as food staples, medicines and salt is inelastic, because people must buy them whatever the price. Demand for luxuries such as jewellery is elastic, because they can be done without.

3. **Proportion of income spent on the good.** If the good takes only a small part of income (a box of matches), a price rise is hardly noticed and demand is inelastic. If it takes a large part of income (a television set), consumers react strongly and demand is elastic.

4. **Time period.** In the short run consumers cannot easily change their habits, so demand is inelastic. Over a longer time they find substitutes, so demand becomes more elastic.

(Other correct points: habit or addiction, such as cigarettes, which makes demand inelastic; and how widely the good is defined, since demand for "food" is less elastic than demand for one brand of biscuit.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
Explain Two (02) determinants of price elasticity of supply.

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Price elasticity of supply measures how much the quantity supplied changes when the price changes. Two determinants are the following.

1. **Time period.** In the short run, supply is inelastic, because producers cannot quickly change their output. For example, a farmer who plants cocoa trees has to wait several years before a rise in the price can increase the output. In the long run, producers can build new factories, plant more crops and hire more labour, so supply becomes more elastic.

2. **Spare capacity and stocks.** If firms have unused machines and workers, or large stocks of finished goods, they can raise supply quickly when the price rises, so supply is elastic. If firms are already producing at full capacity, or if the good is perishable and cannot be stored (fresh tomatoes), supply is inelastic.

(Other correct determinants: mobility of factors of production, which makes it easy to switch resources to the good; ease of storage; and the nature of production, since manufactured goods are easier to increase than agricultural ones.)
